Herman Witsius
WIT-see-uhs
proper noun (person)
Dutch Reformed theologian (1636-1708), author of The Economy of the Covenants Between God and Man.

See also: Herman Witsius

Biblical Definition

Herman Witsius was a Dutch Reformed theologian and professor, one of the most learned and irenic divines of the Further Reformation, best known for his masterwork The Economy of the Covenants Between God and Man. In it he set out the whole plan of salvation under the framework of the covenants: the covenant of works made with Adam, broken by the fall, and the covenant of grace established in Christ, with the eternal covenant of redemption between the Father and the Son as its foundation. Witsius held together what lesser men divided — rigorous doctrine and warm experiential piety, careful scholarship and tender devotion. He labored as a peacemaker in the bitter disputes between the so-called antinomians and neonomians, seeking to honor both free grace and the necessity of holiness without surrendering either to error. His writing is marked by reverence, balance, and a deep savor of communion with God. Witsius stands in the dictionary as the great expositor of covenant theology, who taught the church to read the whole of Scripture as the unfolding of God's covenant dealings, and who joined the precision of the scholastic to the warmth of the godly heart.

Webster 1828 Definition

HERMAN WITSIUS, proper noun. Dutch Reformed theologian and professor (1636-1708).

Author of The Economy of the Covenants Between God and Man.

Expounded the covenants of redemption, works, and grace.

An irenic peacemaker in the antinomian and neonomian disputes.

Joined scholastic precision to warm, experiential devotion.

Key Scripture

Gen 2:17 — "But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die."

Jer 31:33 — "But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people."

Heb 8:6 — "But now hath he obtained a more excellent ministry, by how much also he is the mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises."

Gal 3:17 — "And this I say, that the covenant, that was confirmed before of God in Christ, the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul, that it should make the promise of none effect."

Modern Corruption

Witsius's legacy is honored by recovering covenant theology as the framework of Scripture and by refuting the caricature of Reformed scholasticism as cold, against an age that severs doctrine from devotion.

expand to see more

Dead-orthodoxy caricature. Reformed scholastics like Witsius are often dismissed as dry and lifeless, their precision mistaken for coldness. Witsius himself refutes the slander: his covenant theology breathes reverence and communion, and his learning served piety, not pride. The dictionary holds that sound doctrine and warm devotion are not enemies; the most exact theology, rightly held, kindles the deepest love for God, and Witsius is a model of the union the church must recover.

Covenant-flattened misreading. Some read Scripture as a loose collection of stories and rules, missing the covenantal structure that binds it into one redemptive plan. Witsius recovers the unity: from the covenant of works with Adam to the covenant of grace in Christ, grounded in the eternal covenant of redemption, the Bible tells one story of God keeping covenant with His people. The dictionary commends covenant theology as a faithful key to the whole of Scripture, exalting the faithfulness of the covenant-keeping God.
